source.title: Double and Single Descent in Causal Inference with an Application to High-Dimensional Synthetic Control
source.authors: Jann Spiess; G. Imbens; A. Venugopal

record.tranche_reason: The study tests complexity-risk patterns in linear regression and synthetic control, and explicitly finds single descent rather than double descent for its synthetic-control application.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own empirical complexity sweeps for linear regression and synthetic control. The linear-regression estimates are averaged over five random feature orderings; the synthetic-control estimates average over donor-unit combinations. The coefficient-norm plot is not a test-error result and is not recorded as a row. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own complexity sweeps in a new setting (causal-inference imputation). It finds a double-descent curve for minimal-norm linear regression as covariates pass n. Synthetic control shows only a single monotone descent. Both bear on V4's claim that the double-descent curve holds across model classes.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors show double descent for interpolating linear regression and single descent for synthetic control in their examples. They explain the continuing returns to complexity in both cases by a mechanical model-averaging property: complex models are convex averages of simpler ones. They also give a high-level risk bound under a permutation assumption. They note that the examples are extreme, that the assumptions are high-level, and that primitive conditions (especially on bias) need more work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses minimal-norm linear regression on engineered covariates and synthetic control over donor units, rather than deep-network size sweeps. It varies covariate or donor-set size and measures imputation error; it does not test epoch-wise descent or training-sample-size increases.
record.method_sensitivity: The linear-regression curves are averaged across five random feature orderings and shown separately for CPS and NSW evaluation data and for m = 1, 5, 50, and 100. The synthetic-control result is a sweep over donor combinations; the paper also reports a qualitatively similar robustness check with 10 pre-treatment periods and a larger donor pool.

fits_no_version.finding: The average coefficient norm grows up to the interpolation threshold, peaks at ℓ = n, and then declines mechanically (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter norm of minimal-norm interpolators peaks at the interpolation threshold and falls beyond it.

record.problems: The empirical examples are described by the authors as extreme: the linear-regression application constructs thousands of low-signal covariates, and the main synthetic-control example uses only three training periods and a randomly selected donor pool. The plotted error values are not numerically tabulated in the text; the linear-regression curves average five feature orderings, and the supplied text does not report uncertainty intervals for these curves.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant test-error or imputation-risk rows were omitted. The coefficient-norm result in Figure 3 is not a test-error measure.

untested.parts: No deep networks; the sweeps cover linear regression and synthetic control only.
Training size is fixed (n = 3000). The m values are evaluation subset sizes, not training samples.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of the peak across axes.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple peaks, and no tuned-regularization sweep. Min-norm selection is used only to break ties.
Complexity is not re-counted with an effective-parameter measure.

missing.what: Comparison of interpolating models with a low-dimensional regression on the original covariates: the m = 50 and m = 100 curves reach minima below the dashed baseline lines. This bears on the size of the second descent.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: the study is a new-setting demonstration rather than an argument that V4 is wrong. The synthetic-control label was softened from challenges to limits_scope, because the post-threshold improvement V4 names still holds and only the peak is missing. Propositions 1–5 are theoretical (model averaging, variance reduction beyond n) and are not rows. The theory is listed as originals-adjacent prior work, not as an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Changing training-sample size near an interpolation threshold. The m values in the linear-regression results are evaluation-sample sizes, not training-sample sizes.
The results concern particular linear-regression and synthetic-control applications; they do not establish a pattern across all model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
No test of label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
No test of whether counting effective parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: synthetic control estimator
rows.size_stated: 20 control states in the donor pool; T = 3 pre-treatment years
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of included control states and averaged error across all combinations at each size.

conditions.value: number of control states varied from 1 to 20

rows.note: The authors state that average RMSE decreases monotonically as control units increase, with no intermittent increase or regime change after the number of units passes T = 3; they call this single descent.
rows.check: Error keeps decreasing past the point where some models interpolate, so the improvement V4 describes beyond the threshold is present. There is no peak or U-shape, and the authors call it single descent with no regime change at T = 3. 'Absent' overstates the case against V4: only the peak and first-regime trade-off are missing. Interpolation is also not guaranteed here because the weights are convex.

rows.subject: synthetic control estimator
rows.size_stated: 50 available donors; up to 10,000 donor combinations considered at a complexity level
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of included donor states in a robustness check with more pre-treatment periods.
rows.note: The paper says the robustness-check results are qualitatively similar to Figure 6; the figure plots out-of-time and training RMSE.
rows.check: This is the 10-period robustness check, which the authors call qualitatively similar to Figure 6: a monotone single descent with no peak. The same reasoning as r10 applies.

relationships.condition: Minimal-norm linear regression for wage and ATE imputation (CPS training, NSW/CPS evaluation, m = 1–100)
relationships.reason: The text says error peaks sharply at ℓ = n and then decreases again throughout (r2–r9). For NSW, the second-descent minimum is below the left-side minimum.
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked sharply at ℓ=n and declined beyond it, with the NSW second-descent minimum below the minimum before interpolation.

relationships.condition: Synthetic control with convex weights (California smoking; T = 3 with 20 donors, and T = 10 with 50 donors)
relationships.reason: Risk keeps improving as donors are added, but there is no peak near the interpolation point and no U-shaped first regime (r10, r11). The curve in this model class is single, not double, descent.
relationships.display_finding: Adding donors continued improving risk without a peak near interpolation or a U-shaped first regime.
